Emma Tucker
 
Nvidia’s Strong Results Do Little to Settle Questions About Its Future
 
Plus, parents spend a fortune to turn 6-year-olds into F1 drivers, and a cascade of outages triggers conspiracy theories—and finger pointing
 
 
JASON HENRY FOR WSJ
 

1. FROM MY DESK

 

Nvidia posted another quarter of record-breaking sales that handily beat Wall Street expectations Tuesday—amid a scandal that has rocked the company, taken down its celebrity chief executive and rattled global markets.

 

Just hours before the results were announced, we reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia. That probe deepens the crisis facing the chip maker.

 

Still, investors are squarely focused on how the company will perform going forward. We asked three everyday shareholders what they think about the stock now. Read Oyin Adedoyin’s conversations with them.

 

This is an edition of The 10-Point newsletter, a guided tour of the best coverage in The Wall Street Journal. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here. If you’re reading this in your inbox, tap the headline above for online and audio versions of this newsletter.

 
 
 

2. TODAY’S HEADLINES

 

• Some of President Trump’s political allies are frustrated with the government’s response to a series of high-profile outages that hit email systems, banks and airports. We look at what’s behind the disruptions.

 

• Democrat Mary Peltola unseated Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan of Alaska to become the first Alaska Native elected to the U.S. Senate.

 

• The Trump administration is pulling the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid signs she lacks the support to get confirmed by the Senate.

 

• Trump has landed in Shenzhen ahead of his trilateral meeting with China’s Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. The U.S. is entering an unprecedented three-way nuclear rivalry with the two leaders’ countries.

 

• French far-right leader Marine Le Pen’s commanding lead in the presidential race has set off a push to fill vital gaps in the EU’s finances.

 

• The U.S.’s loss of measles-elimination status is a massive public-health defeat that begs a question: How long will it take to regain it?

 
 
 

3. LIVE FROM THE MARKETS

• Meet the seven Anthropic founders who are about to become multibillionaires.

4. READ IT HERE FIRST

 

The Pentagon urgently needs more Patriot missiles. It’s running into a rayon problem.

 

Only one carbonized rayon product is approved for use in the most advanced Patriot missiles, and it comes from the Kansas factory of a single supplier, Park Aerospace. With stockpiles shrinking, a senior Pentagon official pushed the company for more rayon to help increase production. It soon became clear that Park’s hands were tied. The struggle to find enough rayon for Patriot missiles is emblematic of the challenges the U.S. faces in quickly surging production of critical munitions, report Niharika Mandhana, Josh Chin and Drew FitzGerald.

 

5.

 

Mary Barra transformed GM. Her successor may have to do it again.

 

General Motors’ chief executive hopes to usher in a new era for the 118-year-old automaker. Its move to the tech-focused Nasdaq exchange symbolized Mary Barra’s longtime goal for the company: to be ranked among giants such as Apple and Tesla, not just as an old-line industrial. It could be seen as a crowning achievement ahead of Barra’s possible departure. GM is working with an executive search firm to identify its next CEO, according to people familiar with the matter. That leader could face a thornier road, report Sharon Terlep and Patrick George.

6. SEE THE STORY

 

Parents are spending fortunes to turn 6-year-olds into F1 drivers.

 
 
SAM HAYES FOR WSJ. MAGAZINE
 

Private tracks are popping up around the U.S. to support a growing interest in youth karting. Over the past decade, Formula One has gone from a European motor sport to a lifestyle brand that has spread throughout American culture. Karting, where drivers zoom around in open-cockpit racing vehicles, is seen as an on-ramp for children who dream of becoming the next Lewis Hamilton. Some American families are uprooting to be close to tracks and programs where their children can get the best shot at going pro.

 
 
 

7. HAPPENING TODAY

 

• House Democrats hold a closed-door caucus vote on House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’s bid for speaker.

 

• Nvidia’s interim CEO Colette Kress is scheduled to host a companywide meeting for employees.

 

• The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit begins in Shenzhen, China. 

 

• Economy & Fed: The Commerce Department releases October housing starts, and the Federal Reserve publishes minutes from its Oct. 28 meeting.

 

• Earnings: Target, Lowe’s, TJX, Progressive, Palo Alto Networks

 

• 📰 Today’s paper

 
 
 

8. THE NUMBER

 
150
 

That’s roughly the number of shortened bachelor’s programs announced this year, up from five in 2024, according to Rand senior policy researcher Jason Lee. Many came at the encouragement, or even mandate, of state governing bodies as families question the return on pricey four-year degrees amid mounting student debt. Proponents say three-year bachelor’s programs, often in career tracks such as hospitality or nursing, help meet pressing workforce needs.

 
 
 

9. AND FINALLY…

 

Meet the cycling huntress on a mission to make grown men cry.

 

For Laini Ritsch Multer, the best workout starts with spite and, ideally, ends with a grown man crying. Her hunting ground is Strava—the fitness-tracking network where athletes compete on public leaderboards for “segments,” stretches of road or trail with public leaderboards. The 29-year-old competitive cyclist in Golden, Colo., has a simple objective: Scout the reigning man, chase his ghost and swipe his digital crown. No patch of asphalt is too obscure.
